column4: The section glosses its root ذ ك ر as fame and praise; the Quran calls this a remembrance “for you and your people” (لذكر لك ولقومك) and says they will be questioned about it, giving the Prophet’s elevated mention a communal horizon.

The section joins its root ر ف ع, raising, to ذ ك ر, remembrance; this verse joins houses being raised with His name being mentioned in them (أن ترفع ويذكر فيها اسمه), picturing honor enacted in a place of worship.

The section’s verb و ض ع means setting something down, and 94:2 sets a burden off the Prophet; here the Messenger “removes from them their burden and shackles” (يضع عنهم إصرهم والأغلال), extending that concrete release to his followers.

The section’s burden word وِزْر and the back ظَهْر meet their reversal at the Hour: deniers “carry their burdens on their backs” (يحملون أوزارهم على ظهورهم), making the back bear what 94 says was taken off it.

The section defines roots و ض ع and ر ف ع as opposites; this verse uses both in one ordered scene, raising the heaven and setting down the balance (والسماء رفعها ووضع الميزان). The different objects clarify how opposed motions can serve distinct purposes.

The section’s dictionary gloss ص د ر includes the head place of an assembly, and its root ر ف ع includes raising in rank; after believers make room in gatherings, this verse says God raises believers and knowledge-holders by degrees (يرفع الله ... درجات), joining the two details.

Moses asks his Lord, “open my chest” (رب اشرح لي صدري), using the same chest image as 94:1. The petition places the opening in preparation for a difficult commission, while 94 recalls it as a granted favor.

The section’s opening-chest image has a direct reversal here: God opens a person’s chest to Islam, but makes another’s chest tight and constricted (يشرح صدره للإسلام ... يجعل صدره ضيقا حرجا). It shows the same inner capacity as both gift and deprivation.

The section’s chest image and raised remembrance meet in this address about revelation: “let there be no tightness in your chest about it” (فلا يكن في صدرك حرج منه), then the verse calls the Book a reminder for believers (وذكرى للمؤمنين). It links the Prophet’s ease to the message he carries.

The section recalls the Prophet’s chest opened and burden removed; here God says He knows the Prophet’s chest tightens at what people say (يضيق صدرك بما يقولون). The shared addressee makes this a precise counter-scene of distress caused by speech.

The section describes a burden lifted from the Prophet; this address says the Quran was not sent down to make him miserable (ما أنزلنا عليك القرآن لتشقى), a direct statement of relief in the same prophetic address.

The preceding 20:2 says the Quran was not sent to distress the Prophet; this verse’s own contribution is to call it a reminder (إلا تذكرة لمن يخشى), connecting the section’s lifted burden and raised ذ ك ر to the message’s purpose.

The section treats ذ ك ر as something bestowed for the Prophet; after recounting earlier peoples, this verse says, “We have given you from Us a reminder” (وآتيناك من لدنا ذكرا), a direct parallel in speaker, recipient, and gift.

The preceding 20:99 identifies the gift as a reminder; this verse’s own claim is that whoever turns away from it carries a burden on Judgment Day (فإنه يحمل يوم القيامة وزرا). It makes the section’s pairing of raised remembrance and removed weight consequential in the opposite direction.

The section’s raised-name image is echoed by God making for Abraham’s family “a lofty tongue of truth” (لسان صدق عليا). Here lasting truthful praise is granted to them, matching the section’s link between renown and honor.

Abraham asks God to grant him “a tongue of truth among later generations” (لسان صدق في الآخرين); the prayer anticipates 19:50, where God grants his family a lofty tongue of truth, and makes enduring mention an explicitly requested favor.

The section cites the wording “a book in which is your remembrance” (فيه ذكركم) and notes that ذ ك ر can mean honor as well as recollection. The verse lets the Book carry the community’s remembrance, though that word may also mean admonition.

This verse tells the reader to remember Idris in the Book (واذكر في الكتاب إدريس); its own contribution is the act of textual remembrance, while the next verse, 19:57, says God raised him to a high place, bringing mention and elevation together.

The section stresses that 94:4 raises the Prophet’s name, not his person; here God says He raised Idris to a high place (ورفعناه مكانا عليا). The bodily/person-directed wording provides a specific counter-image, while 19:56 first commands that Idris be remembered in the Book.

The section cites God’s raising some messengers by degrees (ورفع بعضهم درجات); this verse states that He raised some messengers above others in rank, directly locating divine elevation in prophetic status.

After Abraham’s argument against his people, the section cites the declaration “We raise by degrees whom We will” (نرفع درجات من نشاء). It makes rank a divine grant within the very Abraham narrative that frames the section’s comparison.

The section’s root ر ف ع includes elevation of rank; this verse names God “Exalter of degrees” (رفيع الدرجات) and immediately describes revelation being sent to a chosen servant, giving elevation a divine source and prophetic setting.

The section’s elevation vocabulary includes rank; this verse says God has raised some people above others in degrees (ورفعنا بعضهم فوق بعض درجات) while distributing livelihoods, showing social rank as differentiated provision rather than the Prophet’s raised renown.

The section’s root ر ف ع extends to rank; here people are made successors on earth and raised above one another in degrees as a test (ورفع بعضكم فوق بعض درجات ليبلوكم). The verse marks worldly elevation as an allotted trial, distinct from honor in remembrance.

In Joseph’s story, the section’s cited elevation formula recurs: “We raise by degrees whom We will” (نرفع درجات من نشاء). This places divinely granted rank within a scene of judgment and knowledge, broadening the image beyond public fame.

The section pairs lowering a burden with raising a name; this verse describes the Event as lowering and raising (خافضة رافعة). Its reversal makes status unstable at judgment, unlike the specific favor of the Prophet’s enduring mention.

The section’s dictionary gloss ر ف ع includes honor and height; here God says He could have raised a sign-bearer by the signs, but he clung to the earth (لرفعناه بها ولكنه أخلد إلى الأرض). It is a specific reversal of elevation into low attachment.

The section says 94:4 raises the Prophet’s remembrance rather than his person; in Jesus’s address God says, “I will raise you to Me” (ورافعك إلي). Whatever the mechanics of this raising, its grammatical object is Jesus himself, a person-directed counter-image.
The section distinguishes a raised name from a raised person; Joseph seats his parents above him on the throne (ورفع أبويه على العرش), an explicit bodily elevation that sharpens that distinction.

The section’s dictionary gloss of ظ ه ر includes getting on top of something (ظهرت البيت علوته); this verse says the people could not climb over Dhul-Qarnayn’s barrier (فما اسطاعوا أن يظهروه), a concrete limit on rising above an obstacle.

The section’s root ر ف ع includes elevating renown in speech; here good words ascend to God and righteous deeds raise them (إليه يصعد الكلم الطيب والعمل الصالح يرفعه). It makes verbal worth, not bodily height, the thing lifted.

The section’s “for you” raised remembrance is addressed to the Prophet; here God promises to raise him to a praised station (مقاما محمودا). The shared addressee and praise connect enduring honor with an elevated standing.

The section glosses ذ ك ر as renown and praise; this command for believers to invoke blessings on the Prophet gives a concrete communal practice of honoring him, though the verse describes blessings rather than raising his name.

The section’s raised-name image concerns a Prophet known beyond his own time; Jesus announces a messenger after him by name (اسمه أحمد). This is a specific case of a prophetic identity transmitted through earlier speech, not an explicit statement that the name is raised.

The section’s root ذ ك ر includes remembrance as well as renown; here God says, “remember Me, I will remember you” (فاذكروني أذكركم). The reciprocity gives divine remembrance as a distinct form of favor alongside public praise.

The section says the Prophet’s burden was set off him; this verse describes a burdened soul calling another to carry some, but none can carry it, even a close relative (وإن تدع مثقلة إلى حملها لا يحمل منه شيء ولو كان ذا قربى). It sets a boundary: removal of one person’s burden is not transfer to someone else.

The section names the Prophet’s burden as وِزْر; this passage states that no burden-bearer carries another’s burden (ألا تزر وازرة وزر أخرى), making personal responsibility the boundary around the burden removed from him.

The section’s burden word وِزْر is repeated in the rule that no bearer bears another’s burden (ولا تزر وازرة وزر أخرى); this verse sets that rule beside the sending of a messenger, so a burden is accountable to one’s own response to guidance.

In a passage insisting that each soul earns for itself, this verse repeats that no bearer bears another’s burden (ولا تزر وازرة وزر أخرى). It sharpens the section’s “from you” wording as a personal, not transferable, release.

This verse repeats that no burden-bearer carries another’s burden (ولا تزر وازرة وزر أخرى) while saying God has no need of human disbelief; it frames the section’s personal burden as neither shared nor something God needs.

The section’s burden is taken off one person; here those who mislead others are said to carry their own burdens plus additional burdens with them (وليحملن أثقالهم وأثقالا مع أثقالهم). It shows the opposite case where leading others astray adds weight to one’s account.

The section remembers God removing the Prophet’s burden; in this supplication believers ask, “do not place upon us a burden like that laid upon those before us” (ولا تحمل علينا إصرا كما حملته على الذين من قبلنا). It turns relief into a plea that such weight not be imposed.

The section does not identify the Prophet’s burden with revelation, so this is only a possible parallel: God says He will cast upon him a “heavy word” (قولا ثقيلا). It makes prophetic speech a weighty commission, without defining the burden of 94:2.

The section does not say whether its burden is sin, so this remains uncertain; in the same direct address to the Prophet, God promises to forgive his earlier and later wrong (ليغفر لك الله ما تقدم من ذنبك وما تأخر). It offers a specific possible moral counterpart to a burden being removed.

The section’s dictionary gloss for ر ف ع makes elevation the opposite of disgrace; this verse pairs God’s honoring whom He wills with humbling whom He wills (تعز من تشاء وتذل من تشاء), stating that boundary directly.

The section defines elevation against humiliation; this verse says that one whom God humiliates has no one to honor him (ومن يهن الله فما له من مكرم). It makes divine elevation a status no human can confer against God’s judgment.

Like the section’s opened chest, this verse describes a chest opened to Islam and then contrasts it with hearts hardened against God’s remembrance (شرح الله صدره للإسلام ... للقاسية قلوبهم من ذكر الله). It joins chest-capacity to the reception of remembrance.

Moses says his chest is tight and his tongue will not flow (ويضيق صدري ولا ينطلق لساني), a concrete opposite to the section’s opened chest; the speech difficulty also makes bodily capacity relevant to a prophetic commission.

The preceding 15:97 says the Prophet’s chest tightens at what people say; this verse’s own contribution is to command glorification and prostration (فسبح بحمد ربك وكن من الساجدين), placing praise beside that distress and echoing the section’s praise sense of ذ ك ر.

The section’s dictionary form ظهرت على الرجل means prevailing over someone; the youths fear that their people might prevail over them (إنهم إن يظهروا عليكم يرجموكم). It gives a concrete human conflict for the root’s “get above/overcome” sense.

The section’s dictionary branch for ظ ه ر includes prevailing over someone; here God sends the Messenger with guidance and the true religion “to make it prevail over all religion” (ليظهره على الدين كله), applying that root to public triumph.

This verse repeats the section’s root-sense of prevailing: God sent His Messenger with guidance and the true religion “to make it prevail over all religion” (ليظهره على الدين كله). The repeated formulation gives the “rise over” sense a religious and public setting.

The section’s dictionary branch for ظ ه ر includes prevailing over another; this verse again says the Messenger was sent with guidance and truth “to make it prevail over all religion” (ليظهره على الدين كله), a public triumph sense rather than bodily elevation.

The section glosses ذ ك ر as honor and renown; the opening oath calls the Quran “possessor of remembrance” (ذي الذكر). If الذكر here means eminence, it directly parallels raised renown; if it means admonition, the connection is only the shared root.

The section’s dictionary gloss ص د ر includes the foremost part, and its horse example reaches the finish first by its chest; this verse identifies “the foremost” (والسابقون السابقون). It gives a nonlexical Quranic parallel between being first and elevated standing.

The section’s ص د ر dictionary example describes a horse taking the lead with its chest; this verse tells people to race toward forgiveness and a garden (سابقوا إلى مغفرة من ربكم وجنة). The Quran applies forward precedence to seeking divine reward.

The section’s chest-of-the-horse gloss makes first place visible as a race; this verse says that for the lasting reward, competitors should compete (وفي ذلك فليتنافس المتنافسون), a specific moral contest rather than a claim about bodily rank.
